newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Handover discount for HK shares shrinks.
newsitem.headline: Handover discount for HK shares shrinks.

text.p: Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule has served as a drag on its share prices for more than a decade, but with the 1997 handover approaching, the political discount is gradually being reduced, analysts said.

"It has diminished quite a lot," said Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "People are not expecting either side -- as in the British before the handover and the PRC (People's Republic of China) after the handover -- to do anything to rock the boat."
Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng index has risen 11.5 percent since the end of August in what analysts say is a re-rating of the Hong Kong stock market.

Share prices have been trading at around 13 to 14 times earnings but some analysts said rising liquidity, stellar corporate earnings and smoother relations between Hong Kong and China could lift the price earnings multiple to about 16 times.

"There are several things happening in Hong Kong that are pushing it up, but the re-rating in itself hinges on the fact that the market has long required a political risk discount from China," said Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia.

"As 1997 approaches, and it becomes apparent... that China is really not going to be changing things much at all in business conditions, then in fact there is no reason to ask for a political risk discount," he said. "Things will go swimmingly across the handover where business is concerned."

Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities, said historically, Hong Kong shares have traded at about 12 times earnings. "In a very bad year, like 1984 during the Sino-British negotiations, the PE was almost down to seven to eight times."
The Sino-British Joint Declaration was signed on December 19, 1984, ending years of uncertainty as to Hong Kong's future once the British lease on 90 percent of its land mass expired in mid-1997.
The treaty agreed that the entire British colony would be returned to China at midnight on June 30, 1997, and would be permitted to retain its existing freedoms and way of life.

The intervening years have not been smooth, marked by disputes between the two sovereign states on running Hong Kong. Until just a few weeks ago, they could not even agree on the form of a handover ceremony.

But the lowest points -- following China's 1989 crackdown on student-led protests in Beijing and a dispute over electoral reforms in the early 1990s -- have passed and indications of greater cooperation between China and Britain are showing signs of buoying confidence as the handover approaches.
"There is an expectation that the transition will be a fairly seamless occasion," said Pauline Gately, regional strategist at Merrill Lynch.
However, she said while perceptions were changing, the political risks were still there.
"The risk from the political side has always been that China ceases to allow Hong Kong the autonomy that is has enjoyed...Does the political risk change after 1997? No it doesn't," she said.

Analysts say they believe China is keen to show it can engineer a smooth handover and maintain Hong Kong's affluence -- and Hong Kong's exposure to an improving Chinese economy would also be a source of strength for earnings and stocks.

"It is only in the last year that the premium has narrowed and investors have realised that China is not a negative but can be looked at as more of a positive factor," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.
